student_profile.student_background: Conservation rangers and ranger trainees working in wildlife conservancies, actively engaged in human-wildlife conflict mitigation, patrols, and community engagement. Practical field professionals with strong conservation and field knowledge but mixed digital and AI literacy; no programming background assumed. Roughly half are experienced rangers and half are trainees.
student_profile.aggregate_academic_performance: Varied formal education levels; strong practical, applied learning ability. Learn best from concrete, job-relevant examples rather than theory.
student_profile.anticipated_learner_needs_and_barriers: Assume no prior AI experience and uneven typing/device comfort. Connectivity in the field can be limited, so lessons must be self-contained and downloadable, and habits taught should not depend on always-on internet. Use plain language, define every technical term on first use, keep sessions short and practical, and anchor every concept in everyday ranger tasks. English as the working language, kept simple and clear.

instructor_preferences.instructor_emphasis_intent: A practical, self-paced course on using AI assistants to support everyday conservation work. The emphasis throughout is practical problem-solving, NOT teaching AI as a standalone topic — learners should finish feeling confident using AI as a thinking partner for real decisions in their daily work. Each week centers on real ranger tasks: writing incident reports, field documentation, retrieving and verifying information, interpreting simple data, supporting decisions in human-wildlife conflict situations, and drafting community-awareness materials. Emphasize throughout: AI is an assistant, not an authority — outputs must be checked against field knowledge; never enter sensitive or confidential location data (for example the precise positions of endangered animals or anti-poaching operations) into public AI tools; and the ranger's judgment and the chain of command always come first. Stay tool-agnostic: teach generic AI-assistant skills that work with any chat-style AI tool, without endorsing a specific product.
instructor_preferences.instructor_style_preferences: Self-paced delivery: for this pilot the deliverable is high-quality slides plus a detailed speaking script per lesson (the scripts will be used to record short videos in a later stage), followed by a hands-on exercise the learner completes on their own. Open every lesson with a realistic ranger scenario (an elephant crop-raid report, a snare-line patrol log, a community meeting about livestock predation), then teach the skill through that scenario. Short, plain sentences; define terms on first use; frequent worked examples showing a weak AI draft versus an improved one; slides uncluttered and readable on a small screen.
instructor_preferences.instructor_focus_for_assessment: Practical exercises only — no exams. Each week the learner produces a real work artifact (an incident report, a documentation log, a verified information summary, a decision brief, a community flyer draft) using the week's AI skill, and self-checks it against a provided checklist. Feedback from participants is collected each week to improve the course.

course_structure.course_learning_outcomes: Explain in plain language what an AI assistant can and cannot do, and check its outputs against field knowledge; use AI to turn field observations into clear, complete incident reports and patrol documentation; ask effective questions and verify AI-retrieved information before acting on it; use AI to summarize and interpret simple incident data and support — not replace — decisions in human-wildlife conflict situations; draft accurate, respectful community-awareness materials with AI assistance; and apply safe-AI habits consistently: verify outputs, protect sensitive conservation data, and keep human judgment and the chain of command central.
course_structure.weekly_schedule_outline:
AI Basics for Conservation Work: what an AI assistant is and is not, in plain language; what it does well and where it fails (made-up facts, outdated or wrong information); first hands-on conversation with an AI assistant around a simple ranger scenario; the three safety habits — verify, protect sensitive data, keep human judgment central
AI for Incident Reporting: turning rough field notes about a human-wildlife conflict incident (for example an elephant crop raid) into a clear, complete, structured incident report with AI help; what details must never be lost or invented; checking and correcting the AI draft; exercise — write one real-style incident report with AI assistance
AI for Field Documentation: patrol logs, observation records, and photo descriptions; using AI to organize, standardize, and summarize field documentation so it is useful later; keeping records consistent across a team; exercise — convert a week of rough patrol notes into a clean log
Finding and Checking Information with AI: asking good questions about species behavior, regulations, and conflict-mitigation methods; why AI answers must be verified and how to cross-check them; recognizing confident-but-wrong answers; exercise — research a mitigation method with AI and verify each claim before writing a short summary
AI for Data Interpretation and Decision Support: using AI to summarize simple incident data and spot patterns (where and when conflicts cluster); drafting options and trade-offs for a response, with the ranger and chain of command making the decision; the risks of over-trusting AI suggestions; exercise — produce a short decision brief for a recurring conflict situation
AI for Community Materials and the Full Workflow: drafting community-awareness materials (a flyer or talking points about living safely alongside wildlife) that are accurate, respectful, and locally appropriate; capstone — run one incident end-to-end with AI assistance: field notes to report to decision brief to community message, applying all the safety habits; reflection and feedback on the course

assessment_design.assessment_format_preferences: No exams and no coding. Weekly Practical Artifact (60%) — each week the learner produces one job-relevant artifact with AI assistance (incident report, patrol log, verified information summary, decision brief, community flyer) and reviews it against a provided quality-and-safety checklist. Capstone Workflow (30%) — one incident handled end-to-end from field notes to community communication. Participation and Feedback (10%) — brief weekly feedback that is used to improve the course. All assessment is practical and self-paced.
assessment_design.assessment_delivery_constraints: Artifacts are short documents completed offline or on a phone and shared when connectivity allows; checklists are included in the materials so self-assessment does not require internet access.

teaching_constraints.platform_policy_constraints: Materials must be downloadable and usable offline; lessons are recorded from the speaking scripts and distributed as short videos with accompanying slides and exercise sheets. Content must never include or encourage sharing of sensitive conservation data (precise locations of endangered wildlife, anti-poaching operational details) with public AI tools.
teaching_constraints.ta_support_availability: No teaching assistant; the course is self-paced with a local coordinator collecting weekly feedback from participants.
teaching_constraints.instructional_delivery_context: Self-paced professional training for working rangers and trainees in a field setting with limited connectivity; each week is budgeted at 2-3 hours total (lesson, one practical exercise, and a short reflection on applying it to daily work), designed around real conservation tasks rather than classroom activities. Learners have smartphones and can reach a chat-based AI tool when connectivity allows, so exercises are hands-on.

institutional_requirements.program_learning_outcomes: Builds practical AI literacy for a professional conservation workforce, improving the quality and consistency of incident reporting, documentation, and community engagement while establishing safe and responsible AI habits.
institutional_requirements.academic_policies_and_institutional_stan: Content is tool-agnostic and vendor-neutral, uses plain accessible English, respects local community contexts, and treats conservation-sensitive information as confidential — examples never expose real locations of vulnerable wildlife or operational details.
institutional_requirements.department_syllabus_requirements: Required components include learning outcomes, a week-by-week schedule, the practical-exercise approach, and an explicit statement on safe AI use and data protection in conservation work.

prior_feedback.historical_course_evaluation_results: No prior offering; this is the first iteration. The course will be refined iteratively from weekly participant feedback during the pilot.
